newsitem.title: NORWAY: Norway cuts rates, analysts see policy change.
newsitem.headline: Norway cuts rates, analysts see policy change.

text.p: Norway's Central Bank on Friday temporarily gave up the battle to halt a furious rally in the crown in what analysts said could signal a formal shift in currency policy.
Meanwhile, the petrocurrency was expected to continue its climb and some players forecast another cut in interest rates before the market would be satisfied.

"The Central Bank has accepted, at least for the time being, that the market wanted a stronger exchange rate. It is saying it doesn't have the same ambitions for the crown as before," said Harald Magnus Andreassen, chief economist at Elcon Securities.
Norwegian monetary policy has centered on exchange rate stability since the currency was floated at the end of 1992.
But the crown has attracted investors due to the country's booming oil economy which is forecast to show huge surpluses in the national budget and current account this year.

The bank reduced rates for the first time in two years in November in an effort to dampen the crown's ascent. A second cut on Wednesday added fuel to the fire and sent the crown climbing to its strongest level since 1990.

The rise has forced the bank to intervene on the foreign currency market to the tune of 20 billion crowns since the beginning of the year. In Friday's announcement, the Central Bank said it would "significantly reduce" intervention for a period.
Elcon's Andreassen said the market had clearly demonstrated that reasonable interest rates and a stable currency under current monetary policy were untenable.

"We have now seen that the old machine does not work. The bank asked for a change to policy in November. Although it has lost out to the market, maybe we are seeing the first signs of a change, maybe it is now winning against the government," he told Reuters.

Knut Anton Mork, chief economist at Handelsbanken Markets, said the bank looked to be trying the regain control of the money market and had left a door open for another rate cut. But the latest move had still failed to clarify its long-term policy, he said.

"I see this as an attempt to win back control over the debt market. The Central Bank has been trying to control both the foreign exchange and interest rate market and that could not last. The development we see now is a classic example of this,," Mork said.

"It has said it will not intervene but it has not said it is giving up stabilisation of the exchange rate. It can still use interest rates to control the currency, so it is conceivable to have another rate cut."
Analysts said the floating crown was likely to continue although the market could be volatile.

"It means that the crown might be more volatile than we've seen before, that the markets are going to have a closer look at the crown, possibly test it towards the D-mark. We are going to see a new level for the crown," Oystein Stephansen at S-E Banken in Oslo told Reuters Financial Television (RFTV).
In addition the crown now would be subject to volatile swings associated with petrocurrencies and oil prices.

High crude prices often send oil currencies above their long-term equilibriums, weakening the competitiveness of mainland industry and creating uncertainty over the profitability in the exposed sector such as manufacturing.
Mork said it was vital for the bank to try and raise rates as soon as possible to counter inflationary pressures that are creeping into the economy.
The rate cuts would support inflation, although the appreciation in the crown may dampen prices on imports, which in turn could offset domestic prices, Mork said.
He forecast inflation to rise 2.8 percent year-on-year in January. December's figures from the government statistics bureau showed a year-on-year increase of 1.8 percent.
"These are good times for investors in the Norwegian market, but it won't last and I would say: 'Buy, but get ready to sell'."
